Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

locations included Ash Gate, Mill Ford, Alder Slope, Quarry Spur and the east meadow. The cameras were placed on existing paths and crossings, with no new trails cut. It covers August 15 through October 31 at the fictional 640-acre Cedar Run property north of Bellwether, managed by the Cedar Run Land Trust.

Begin with a short opening that gives the review dates. Explain the camera setup in plain language, then describe the records. Keep the limits of the review clear throughout, and focus on the supplied notes.

**Camera setup and review**

Twelve motion-triggered cameras were set out for the review period; ten produced usable image sequences. At Mill Ford, water entered one camera enclosure and its card could not be read. Another camera had a corroded battery tray. There are no usable sequences from those two units.

The ten usable cameras yielded 412 wildlife sequences that could be identified at least broadly. The cameras were placed at Ash Gate, Mill Ford, Alder Slope, Quarry Spur, and the east meadow, on existing paths and crossings. No new trails were cut. Cameras were aimed roughly 45 to 60 centimetres above the ground. They used no bait, recorded 24-second clips when triggered by motion, and used infrared at night. They did not record sound or provide live views. People walked in to retrieve cards and inspect batteries, so the cameras were not continuously watched.

Include Jonah Pike, the reserve manager, in connection with the choice of locations. Use his words exactly: “We chose the old footpaths because they are easy to reach without cutting new trails.” Do not present this as a general claim about every camera location.

**Records and what they show**

The 412 sequences are a tally of sequences, not individual animals: 184 white-tailed deer, 73 raccoon, 41 gray fox, 36 coyote, nine black bear, three bobcat, 52 wild turkey, and 14 unknown wildlife sequences. These figures add to 412. Do not turn them into a population estimate or say that the reserve has that many animals. A repeat appearance may be the same animal, and individuals were not identified. Gray fox figures are sequences, too.

“Unknown wildlife” means that an image clearly showed wildlife but could not be identified more specifically; it does not mean an unknown species was discovered. Explain this without suggesting that the image reviewers were careless. Do not make every species sound equally important or turn the account into a dramatic wildlife-sighting story. You may mention the three bobcat sequences as a limited record, but do not imply bobcats are rare at the reserve or that this was a first sighting.

One bobcat sequence from Alder Slope on October 19 shows part of the animal’s flank and tail. The angle does not establish its age or sex. At Quarry Spur, a black bear appears in three sequences within an 11-minute period on September 28. The records alone cannot establish whether this was one visit or more than one animal. There were also four clips triggered by people walking past. These are separate from the 412 wildlife sequences and should not imply a visitor count. If you mention them, retain both the date and number of clips as given; no date for those clips is supplied. The images do not establish why an animal used a path or where it went afterwards.

**Required numbered section**

Include a section titled “What a camera sequence can tell us,” with exactly three numbered points. Cover these ideas:
1. Repeated clips are not automatically separate animals.
2. A camera records only the short view in front of it.
3. The tally describes sequences collected during this review, not the reserve’s animal population.

**Quotations**

Mara Velez coordinates the volunteers who service the cameras. Include her remarks naturally if they fit, keeping the wording exactly as quoted: “The first week is mostly us learning whether the straps are going to stay put.” This comment concerns checking the installation, not the wildlife tally.

Eli North is the range technician who reviewed image sequences. Use his wording exactly if included: “I don't call two clips two foxes unless we can tell them apart.” This is a caution about identifying separate animals. Mara also said: “A camera sees a crossing, not the whole animal's day.” Keep all supplied quotations as written and use them as ordinary spoken remarks from this review.

Close with an open-ended paragraph. No decision has been made about what monitoring comes next: do not announce a plan, promise another review, or say the project has proved a trend.
